items.title: SASY: Agent Policies in Declarative Logic
items.story_key: story|title:sasy agent policies in declarative logic
items.content_excerpt: SASY checks each action an AI agent takes, such as sending an email or running a command, before it happens. You write the policy as rules in Datalog, a declarative logic language. Each decision takes into account everything that led to that action, from what the agent read to the tools it called. Both runs below give an agent the same task: summarize a report and email the summary to reviewer@example.net. In the second run, the agent also reads an untrusted note telling it to send the summary somewhere else. Your agent runs as before. The SASY SDK records what it reads and produces, and the SASY engine checks each tool call against your policy and that history before it runs. A denied call does not run, and the agent gets the reason. The SDK hooks into LangChain, Google ADK and Langroid automatically. Custom agents use sasy.record and sasy.check_tool_call . Docs Architecture → Blog Agentic Security: An Aspect-Oriented Programming Perspective → Let a coding agent set SASY up for you, or install it by hand in a Python project. The documentation explains how to write policies and add SASY to each framework. A real run of the message-flow example. An agent is asked to email a reviewer a summary of a confidential report. On the way, it reads an untrusted note telling it to send the summary elsewhere, and follows it. That email depends on both the note and the report, and the policy blocks it. The graph is what SASY records for the run. When the agent tries the send, SASY follows the arrows back to both documents, and the policy denies it. SASY Guard brings SASY to the coding agent on your machine. It checks every tool call against a policy and the session's history. Guard blocks things like destructive commands, piping a downloaded script into a shell, or sending data out after reading secrets. then ask your coding agent to set up SASY Guard. It installs everything and tells you how to test it. The tabs show the same steps by hand. Needs Claude Code v2.1.289 or later. The mod shows each decision in the session. In this demo, an agent taken over by a prompt injection reads .env , then tries to send data to an outside server. Guard blocks the command because it traces back to the secret. items.title: Hibana: Fast Agentic Inference on Unified-Memory Devices
items.story_key: story|title:hibana fast agentic inference on unified memory devices
items.content_excerpt: On a unified-memory device, the model and every agent's history share one memory. Hibana co-designs the model, its memory, and its decoding so many agents run fast on a single DGX Spark. Yahya Emara 1* , Chi-Chih Chang 1* , Anthony Fei 1 , Ahmed F. AbouElhamayed 1 , Chong-Yan Chen 2 , Hung-Yueh Chiang 3 , Kai-Chiang Wu 4 , Mohamed S. Abdelfattah 1 1 Cornell University 2 University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign 3 Independent researcher 4 National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University * Equal contribution Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on one DGX Spark, against the fastest of vLLM, llama.cpp, and TensorFold. Local agents extend long histories, pause for tools, and run side by side. On a unified-memory device such as the DGX Spark, the weights, the active requests, and every saved history share one 128 GB pool, and every generated token streams the weights through limited bandwidth. Hibana attacks both limits at once. Model surgery. Edit the trained model to fit the hardware: 3-bit weights, INT8 recurrent state, and a 2-bit draft head, so each token reads fewer bytes. Unified-memory management. Keep every agent's state across turns, spilling it to the SSD when GPU memory runs out, so a returning agent resumes instead of recomputing. Adaptive speculation. Share experts across drafted tokens and draft only as far as acceptance pays for, so each weight read yields more tokens. Decoding one request is bound by memory bandwidth, so the fastest token is the one that reads the fewest bytes. Each group of 32 weights snaps to an 8-entry FP8 codebook, so each weight is stored as a 3-bit index. The kernel looks up the codes and feeds FP8 tensor cores directly. Eight values per group, three bits per weight. Codes take 3 bits and each group of 32 adds one 8-bit scale: 3 + 8/32 = 3.25 bits per weight. The codebook here is fitted to the group for illustration. The drafter's output head scores every token in the vocabulary and is the largest matrix the drafter reads. A 2-bit copy is cheap but noisy, so Hibana uses it only to shortlist candidates, then rescores the shortlist in FP8. Shortlist in 2 bits, decide in FP8. Context: for i in range( . The served head shortlists 16 of over 100,000 tokens and agrees with the FP8 head on 99.76% of tokens. Agents take turns. By the time an agent returns, other agents have usually pushed its state out of GPU memory. Discard an evicted agent's state and its next turn recomputes the whole context. Hibana spills the KV cache, recurrent state, and draft state

items.title: TrustGraph – ACLs that follow the data through your AI agents
items.story_key: story|title:trustgraph acls that follow the data through your ai agents
items.content_excerpt: Policy-as-code for what AI agents produce: decide where an agent's output can go, based on what it read. Policy-as-code for what AI agents produce. Decide where your agent's output can go, based on what it read. Permission systems decide what an agent may read . They lose track the moment the agent writes something new. In May 2025, Invariant Labs showed a coding agent reading a user's private repositories and publishing what it found in a pull request on a public one, after it read a crafted issue. Every step was something the agent was allowed to do. Reading private code was fine. Opening a public pull request was fine. Nothing checked that the second came from the first. Taking away access does not fix this: the agent needs the private code to do its job. What is missing is a rule about where things derived from it may go. The same gap opens each time one agent hands its work to another: the restriction should follow the data through every step. You write one small policy file. It says who may read anything derived from each source, which agents may use it, and where each action sends output: TrustGraph records what each output was built from, through every step, and answers allow , needs approval or deny with the reason: Approval adds a requirement. It never widens who may read a source. Anything the policy does not name is denied. It starts local fake MCP servers and a real gateway, follows an injected instruction in private code, and verifies that the public PR and secret-bearing search queries never reach the upstream. The same agent completes an authorized private PR. Restarting and reconnecting preserves the restrictions; a fresh public-only agent can complete a public task. The printed graph explains SourceCode@1 → first_line_v1 → Summary@1 → denied public PR . No API keys or model service are needed. This deterministic client deliberately attempts the injected action; it does not measure a model's attack success rate. See the protected configuration and threat model . A policy carries its own tests. Each one states what the agent read, what it tries to do and the answer you expect. Read a policy back in plain English, see exactly who gains access when it changes, and run it through the simulator: Every command takes --json . There are six worked policies in examples/policies . TrustGraph assumes an agent drafts the policy and a person approves it. Every problem is reported at once with a path, a stable code and a suggestion, so an agent can run

items.title: MeReader: An Offline, Privacy-Preserving, Progress-Aware AI Assistant for Narrative eBook Reading
items.summary: This paper introduces MeReader, a privacy-preserving, offline and progress-aware AI assistant designed to function as a contextual companion for narrative reading on consumer hardware. Unlike conventional Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems that process documents/books online in an all-texts-at-once type of way, thereby risking narrative spoilers, MeReader confines both retrieval and generation to the reader's distinct position in the text. The system integrates a hybrid retrieval architecture, combining vector similarity, BM25, and summary embeddings, to ensure high fidelity to the reader's current context. We evaluate the system across classical English books using both quantitative comprehension metrics and qualitative LLM-based independent judging. The results identify a quality-latency frontier, showing that mid-sized local models (2b-4b) can achieve comprehension parity with larger counterparts (5b+) while maintaining acceptable response quality. Importantly, the proposed progress-aware boundary mechanism is shown to prevent future content leakage without compromising retrieval quality and correctness. These findings suggest that a localized, privacy-centric approach can augment, rather than replace, the digital reading experience, offering a good alternative to cloud-dependent services. Therein, there remains a lack of amalgamate systems which combine progress-aware, privacy-preserving, and narrative eBook reading with AI support. It is in this very gap that the development of MeReader came to be; synthesizing said strands into an offline, book-constrained assistant focused on enhancing comprehension without compromising narrative continuity or user privacy.

items.title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
items.summary: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $π_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $π_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

items.title: GT-FENG: General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding in Language Models *Author(s)
items.summary: Whether a language model's answer is correct often depends on context: the same value can be right under one jurisdiction, date, or legal definition and wrong under another. We introduce GT-FENG (General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding), the first general framework to unify contextual/temporal correctness and rule-based error attribution across law, policy, and other rule-governed domains. GT-FENG checks answers against the applicable rules and identifies documented rules that match incorrect answers. It shows that when multiple rules give the same value, the answer alone cannot tell which rule the model used. In Medicaid income-limit answers from two models, documenting the asked state's own records reduces the number of wrong answers that match only other states' values by 68-78%, and more than half of stable wrong answers then match two or more documented sources. GT-FENG provides a foundation for evaluating language models in rule-governed domains and for future benchmarks and evaluation toolkits. We release GT-FENG as an open-source Python package, gtfeng.

items.story_key: model:gemini|ver:4|title:introducing gemini 4 hydrogen
items.content_excerpt: Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows. While our frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon , excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of Google AI Studio , the Gemini API, Gemini for business , the Gemini app , Google Search , and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity . Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows. To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity . Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs. Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. The gains come from building on what is new in Rubin: kernels tuned for its split memory and FP4 tensor cores, specialized decode kernels for low latency, and a rack-wide KV cache and Engram tables shared over NVLink. This is the third post in our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash series. The first post covered day-0 bring-up and kernel fusions. The second scaled the model to a GB300 NVL72 rack with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP. This post moves the same stack to Vera Rubin NVL72, which we introduced last month . Rubin opens up new avenues for optimization. We start with the hardware facts that shaped our work, then go through four groups of optimizations: Figure 1: SemiAnalysis AgentX on NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 (vLLM, P/D disaggregation, Wide-EP) vs. GB300 NVL72. Throughput counts cached input, uncached input and output tokens ( GB300 source ). We measure performance with the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark as a representative agentic serving workload, aligned with our previous posts. Figure 1 compares the two racks' raw throughput (total tokens per GPU per second, including input, cached, and output) and power-normalized throughput, respectively in two tabs. We use the same methodology as in our previous GB300 post . For kernels and model forward profiling, vllm bench forward times exact prefill and decode batches through the real execute_model path, with real weights and real AgentX tokens. We A/B prefill kernels in loops that run for several seconds and report sustained numbers where they differ. Three properties of Vera Rubin NVL72 drove most of the decisions below. Where an optimization is specific to Rubin, we say which of them it relies on. Figure 2: Weight stages of the routed-expert GEMM in one SM's shared memory, with the SM100 MXFP8×MXFP4 MMA and with SM107's K64 MXFP8×MXFP4 MMA on packed FP4. items.title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
items.summary: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number $κ$ of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit $κ\rightarrow 1$. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error $\varepsilon$ using $Θ(\logκ\,\log(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most $\varepsilon$ 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d} \, \mathrm{polylog}(κ, 1/\varepsilon))$ score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.

items.title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles
items.summary: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.

items.content_excerpt: The current Claude lineup has four generally available models: Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs. If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code , you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs. The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium . There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work. Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate. Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model. Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page . When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. When you pick a larger model, for example, you are choosing capability over latency. These are the main trade-offs to think through. Generally, bigger models cost more per token and are more capable, but the cost vs capability trade-off isn't universally true at the task level. A higher price per token doesn't always mean a higher cost per task, or a better result. As we showed in Spending your effort , on Anthropic's runs of Terminal-Bench 3.0, the previous Fable, 5.1, at max scored 58.0%, while Opus 5.5 at high scored 58.9% with half the tokens. On the hardest work, the price gap can close. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at high scored about level with Opus 5.5 at max (45.3% vs. 45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task. So before you raise Opus 5.5 past high on a hard task, test Fable 5.2. For everyday work, Opus 5.5 at medium is still the place to start. For benchmark results, see the launch post . However,

items.title: Inkling 2 Small on vLLM: Day-0 Support
items.summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|variant:small|title:inkling 2 small on vllm day 0 support
items.content_excerpt: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small on day 0. It is a multimodal (text and vision) MoE model with 594B total and 17B active parameters and up to 1M tokens of context. The model also comes with a native DSpark speculator. vLLM supports it with optimized performance (up to 630 TPS/user at TP4 and acceptance length 3.5) and also supports LoRA. Figure 1. Inkling 2 Small architecture. Gold marks what is new or changed since Inkling. Inkling backbone + recent advances. Inkling 2 Small keeps Inkling's backbone: the 5:1 mix of sliding-window and full attention, GQA with a learned relative bias instead of RoPE, the four short convolutions per layer and a sigmoid-routed MoE. On top of it, it adds recent advances. Block attention residuals replace the residual stream, so before each sublayer a learned query mixes the outputs of earlier 6-layer blocks. Gated attention puts a sigmoid gate on each head's output, together with a per-token attention sink . It replaces the hMLP image encoder with a 23-layer ViT. Mixed-precision MoE with Four-Over-Six NVFP4. Out of Inkling 2 Small's 48 layers, the experts of the first 40 use NVFP4 and those of the last 8 use MXFP8. The NVFP4 activations use a per-token global scale plus dual-candidate block scales ( Four Over Six ): for each 16-element block, the quantizer tries scaling the block's maximum to 6 and to 4, and keeps whichever gives the lower reconstruction error (MAE). DSpark speculator with an RNN head. The checkpoint also ships a DSpark draft in place of Inkling's 8 chained MTP heads. The speculator has 5 layers and drafts 7 tokens per step. The head is the RNN variant that DeepSeek's DSpark paper described. Kernel fusion and PDL. vLLM aggressively fuses the collective communication and memory-bound ops between sublayers into a single kernel. With attention residuals, each boundary needs an all-reduce, a short convolution, a residual update, the attention-residual mix and an RMSNorm: five memory-bound steps on the same hidden states. The fused kernel, allreduce_conv_mix (gold in Figure 2), runs the all-reduce over NVLink multicast and keeps everything after it in registers. The GEMM, attention, routing and activation kernels launch with programmatic dependent launch (PDL), so each one's prologue overlaps the tail of the previous kernel, which matters at small batch sizes, where a decode step is a long chain of short kernels. items.summary: Every team has “recipes” that govern how they work. The way finance puts together...
items.story_key: story|title:teach genie one your workflows the ultimate guide for skills in genie one
items.content_excerpt: How to turn the way you work into repeatable skills that Genie One can run for you Every team has “recipes” that govern how they work. The way finance puts together the month-end pack, the checks sales operations runs before a forecast call, the format leadership expects when performing a retrospective. These templates live in people's heads, in old emails and in "here's how I do it" documents that nobody can find. Genie One already understands a lot about your business. Through Genie Ontology , it not only learns your business definitions, but also how your teams use their data. Skills add an extra layer of control: how you like things done. A skill is a workflow recipe that Genie One can follow on demand ensuring a consistent format and output each time. For example, with a skill, users can prompt Genie One to "Put together our trading report for last month", and know that it will return the report the way your team would have prepared it, with the same checks, the same structure and the same level of detail. Genie One leverages skills when they are either called directly by the user, or when it decides that it's relevant to what you've requested. That means you can keep adding skills, each with as much detail as its task needs, and their guidance stays with that task rather than spilling into your other work. Skills are durable, reusable assets. A skill is a written record of how your team works, in plain language and in the open Agent Skills format, so it's yours to keep, review and build upon. Publish it through Unity Gateway and the same recipe can be used by any agent that supports MCP, including the coding agents your teams already use. And once it works, share it across your organisation, so one person's best way of working becomes everyone's. It’s easy to get started with skills. You can build a skill directly in Genie One through one conversation, simply by explaining your workflow in detail once. You should consider a skill when you find yourself explaining the same thing to Genie One more than once. Good signs include: A skill holds the method: the steps, checks and format for a piece of work. Genie Ontology tells Genie One what things mean, and a skill tells it a specific way to get something done. Skills also work hand in hand with Genie Agents . items.title: Kitesurf is now open source
items.summary: Kitesurf, our experimental browser engine for AI agents, is now open source. Inspect the code, run it locally, or deploy your own instance on Cloudflare Workers.
items.story_key: story|title:kitesurf is now open source
items.content_excerpt: We introduced Kitesurf , our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer. Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network. Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation. Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly: These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices. Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result. All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together. To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements , then clone the repository , install dependencies, and start the engine: The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787 . Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically. Or you can point your AI harness at the local CDP port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf.
